name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,136

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A Henry James novel that’s mere rubbish

indicators.note: as a verb, to rubbish something is to trash it, so the letters before it get wrecked and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A dismissive critic sneers that some Henry James novel is worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a novel by James; the answer is Colm Tóibín's 2004 novel about him, a book with Henry James as its hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Tóibín's fictional portrait of the American-born writer in his later London years carries that title, so it is literally a novel about him.

clue.text: Sort to confront one such as Miller or Franklin?

definitions.text: one such as Miller or Franklin?

blocks.note: a sort or kind
to face someone is to confront them

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to stand up to a person such as Arthur Miller or Benjamin Franklin.
explanation.walkthrough: Miller and Franklin look like the playwright and the statesman, but here they are fonts: Miller and Franklin Gothic. A 'sort' is also a single piece of printer's type.
explanation.definitionFit: Miller and Franklin Gothic are named printing fonts, each an example of a designed lettering style.

clue.text: Poor Tom Wolfe had at last turned around paper

indicators.note: 'at last' points to the final letter of each word in front of it
something turned around faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: final letters of the two words
a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper

explanation.surface: The novelist Tom Wolfe, poor fellow, finally had a newspaper turn against him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom Wolfe' reads as one name, but 'Poor Tom' belongs to the definition and Wolfe starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: In King Lear, Gloucester's son disguises himself as the mad beggar Poor Tom, so this is the character's assumed identity.

clue.text: Writer with licence to cover missing husband

indicators.note: what is missing has been left out, so one letter is dropped

blocks.note: 'and' means together with
reg is short for a car's registration, the number on its licence plate
to hide something is to cover it
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: An author is licensed to stand in for an absent husband.
explanation.walkthrough: HIDE loses its H to leave IDE; the French novelist's name then assembles from AND, REG and IDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Gide was a French novelist and Nobel laureate, author of The Immoralist and The Counterfeiters.

clue.text: Bottom lover I spank in Taiwan on and off

indicators.note: switching on and off means every other letter is kept
one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
to tan someone's hide is to beat them
first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A rude confession: someone who likes bottoms admits to spanking now and then in Taiwan.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottom is the weaver in A Midsummer Night's Dream, not a body part; to tan a hide is old slang for a thrashing.
explanation.definitionFit: The fairy queen, under Oberon's love potion, dotes on the weaver Bottom while he wears an ass's head.

clue.text: “There was an awful — once in heaven” (Keats)

definitions.text: “There was an awful — once in heaven” (Keats)

blocks.clueFragment: “There was an awful — once in heaven”
blocks.note: the quotation with one word removed
the source: Keats's narrative poem Lamia, Part 2

explanation.walkthrough: Keats complains that cold philosophy will 'unweave' this once-awesome sight, now catalogued as mere optics.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats laments that science has explained the arc of colours after rain, robbing it of the awe it once inspired.

clue.text: Bunch of plums reported by Morse and Lewis?

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so its sound matters, not its spelling

blocks.note: Morse and Lewis are the police detectives of the Oxford TV series

explanation.surface: A tip-off about some plums is passed to the Oxford detectives.
explanation.walkthrough: Plums here are the trees, not the fruit; Inspector Morse and his sergeant Lewis are policemen in Colin Dexter's novels and the TV dramas.
explanation.definitionFit: A small group of trees growing together is called a copse, so several plum trees would form one.

clue.text: Short piece of work about current musical group

indicators.note: cut short, the word loses its final letter
going about something means surrounding it

blocks.note: a chore, shortened
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A short composition about present-day music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of work' suggests a composition, but it is a chore; I sits inside CHOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A body of singers who perform together is a classic example of an ensemble of musicians.

clue.text: Novelist and MP mixed up with Olivier

indicators.note: things mixed up are jumbled into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A novelist and a Member of Parliament get embroiled with the actor Laurence Olivier.
explanation.walkthrough: An MP is a Member of Parliament, here simply two letters to scramble.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian chemist and Auschwitz survivor wrote fiction such as If Not Now, When? as well as memoirs.

clue.text: Some bootleg Gershwin, a self-professed genius

indicators.note: 'some' takes just part of the words that follow

blocks.note: found spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A pirated Gershwin recording, Gershwin himself being a man who claimed to be a genius.
explanation.walkthrough: The genius is not Gershwin but Dave Eggers, whose memoir is titled A Heartbreaking Work of Staggering Genius.
explanation.definitionFit: The American author's memoir title proclaims his own staggering genius, half in jest.

clue.text: Called for Duke to go after Cesario

blocks.note: in Twelfth Night, Viola disguises herself as the page Cesario
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: In Twelfth Night, Cesario is summoned to attend the Duke Orsino.
explanation.walkthrough: Duke Orsino does call for Cesario in the play, which makes the surface feel like plot summary.
explanation.definitionFit: To page someone is to summon them by calling their name, as in a hotel or over a loudspeaker.

clue.text: Men involved in following Pendel’s pursuit

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it

blocks.note: tailing someone is following them
OR, other ranks, means ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Some men are caught up in tracking a character named Pendel.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Pendel is le Carré's The Tailor of Panama, a spy who is a tailor by trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Pendel's trade, making and fitting suits, is the craft of cutting cloth for clothes.

clue.text: Price performing without Jack, a kid’s author

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a fare is the price of a journey
a show that is on is being performed
J is the card abbreviation for jack

explanation.surface: A man called Price, performing without his partner Jack, is a children's writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but has its old sense of outside. Eleanor Farjeon wrote Morning Has Broken and many children's stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor Farjeon was a celebrated English writer of stories and verse for young readers.

clue.text: One of the first Scots poets listening to Figaro?

definitions.text: One of the first Scots poets

indicators.note: when listening, you register the sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: Figaro is The Barber of Seville in Rossini's opera

explanation.surface: An early Scottish poet is pictured enjoying an aria from Figaro.
explanation.walkthrough: John Barbour wrote The Brus in the 1370s, one of the earliest works of Scots poetry; in a British accent his name and Figaro's trade are said alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbour's epic about Robert the Bruce is among the earliest surviving long poems in the Scots language.

clue.text: Churchman with line in any Oscar Wilde novel

indicators.note: something novel is new, so the letters form a new word

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clergyman is mentioned in a line of some Oscar Wilde novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like Wilde's book (he wrote only one), but it is the anagram signal meaning new.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Wolsey was Henry VIII's archbishop and Lord Chancellor, a prince of the Roman Catholic church.

clue.text: Sheridan plays about love of the old country

indicators.note: plays are acted out, so the letters are performed in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
love is nil in tennis scoring, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Sheridan's comedies concern a love of one's native land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sheridan plays' suggests The Rivals or The School for Scandal; the name is instead fodder, with O worked in.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodesia was a southern African state that became Zimbabwe in 1980, so it is a former nation no longer on maps.

clue.text: He travelled by transport and field, I’m told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so sound counts over spelling

blocks.note: a lorry is the British word for a truck
a lea is a poetic word for a meadow

explanation.surface: A traveller says he got about by vehicle and on foot across fields.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurie Lee walked out of Gloucestershire and across Spain, recounted in As I Walked Out One Midsummer Morning.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Cider with Rosie famously tramped through 1930s Spain playing his violin, a writer known for journeying.

clue.text: Val’s collection gets Time’s dander up

indicators.note: something stirred up is agitated and thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time, plus the S of the possessive
taken as written

explanation.surface: Somebody named Val's anthology annoys Time magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Val is the crime writer Val McDermid, and this is the title of her 2005 short-story collection; to get one's dander up is to lose one's temper.
explanation.definitionFit: McDermid's first book of short crime stories was published under that title, so it names her collection.

clue.text: Characters one may hear on a radio play

definitions.text: Characters one may hear on a radio

blocks.clueFragment: Characters one may hear on a radio
blocks.note: first meaning: two words of the radio spelling alphabet, standing for the letters R and J
second meaning: Shakespeare's tragedy of star-crossed lovers

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a radio drama; but 'characters' are letters, and radio operators spell R and J with these code words.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet two letters are spoken as the lovers' names, and together they title Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: One helping a person like Chinaski?

blocks.note: first meaning: an accomplice who assists
second meaning, split as two words: a gambler

explanation.walkthrough: Henry Chinaski, Charles Bukowski's alter ego, spends his days betting at the racetrack, so he is a gambler; split differently, the word means an accomplice.
explanation.definitionFit: One who assists a crime is an accomplice; read as two words it describes a racetrack gambler like Bukowski's hero.

clue.text: Pair not finishing game, Robert Browning’s last?

indicators.note: a word not finishing stops short of its final letter

blocks.note: a duo, cut short
chess is a game

explanation.surface: A couple abandon a match, and the poet Browning's final words follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' suggests Browning's final work, but it is the last word of his poem My Last Duchess.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's dramatic monologue My Last Duchess ends its title with this noble rank, so it is literally the title's last word.

clue.text: One done in by two acts in party uprising

indicators.note: one piece placed inside another
in a down entry, rising means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: a do is a party
acts of parliament are laws, plural for two

explanation.surface: Someone is killed by a pair of revolts during a political party coup.
explanation.walkthrough: The plays' 'two acts' are laws; Lee Harvey Oswald was himself shot dead by Jack Ruby, and Oswald in King Lear is killed by Edgar.
explanation.definitionFit: Kennedy's assassin was himself shot two days later, so he is someone who was killed.

clue.text: Criminals getting staff to circulate cop’s ends

indicators.note: the two letters that begin and end a police officer's title move round and trade places

blocks.note: a sceptre is a ruler's ceremonial staff

explanation.surface: Crooks get a staff member to pass round a police officer's leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the C and P change places, the first and last letters of 'cop'. SPECTRE is the villainous organisation in Ian Fleming's Bond stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bond villains' criminal syndicate, led by Blofeld, goes by this acronym name.

clue.text: This publication abridged cracking Bond book

indicators.note: an abridged text has been cut, so a letter goes
to crack something is to break into it

blocks.note: TLS, the Times Literary Supplement, shortened
a tie is a bond

explanation.surface: The TLS publishes a shortened version of a James Bond novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond book' suggests Fleming; Bond is a tie and 'book' is the definition. 'This publication' is the TLS, where the puzzle appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Publishers count each book they issue as a title, as in 'a list of new titles'.

clue.text: Revolutionary artist capturing setter’s wild fancy

indicators.note: to capture is to take and hold, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: Che Guevara, the Argentine revolutionary
the setter is 'I', so setter's is I'M (I am)
RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: A radical painter captures the crossword compiler's crazy whim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like an adjective for the artist, but it is Che on his own.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is an illusion or fanciful idea, from the mythical fire-breathing hybrid monster.

clue.text: Bit of editorial work written up by her?

definitions.note: a pronoun standing for the female novelist

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small part, here its opening letter
in a down entry, going up means letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: opening letter
toil is hard work

explanation.surface: A snippet of editorial work, penned by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Her' is George Eliot, Mary Ann Evans, a woman who wrote under a man's name; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot was the pen name of the Victorian novelist Mary Ann Evans, so the masculine name hides a woman.

clue.text: TS Eliot works on a Republican thinker

indicators.note: something worked is reshaped, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
R stands for Republican
taken as written

explanation.surface: T.S. Eliot writes about a philosopher of republics, perhaps Plato.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' looks like Eliot's oeuvre but is the anagram signal; 'Republican thinker' tempts towards Plato, author of The Republic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek philosopher, pupil of Plato and tutor to Alexander, is a founding figure of Western thought.

clue.text: Children’s author to call back about second part of Crusade?

indicators.note: the second part of a word is its second letter
going back means the letters run in the opposite direction
going about something means surrounding it

blocks.note: to dial is to call on the phone
the second letter

explanation.surface: A writer for children recalls a sequel about the Crusades.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Laird writes children's novels, including Crusade (2007), which makes the surface almost literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Laird is a British author of books for young readers such as Red Sky in the Morning.

clue.text: Desperate chap with note for underworld reporter?

blocks.note: Desperate Dan is the strongman cowboy in the British comic The Dandy
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A desperate man has a message for a journalist covering organised crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld reporter' suggests a crime correspondent, but it is the poet who described Hell in the Inferno.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante's Inferno narrates his journey through Hell, so he reports from the realm of the dead.

clue.text: “As jewels lose their glory if neglected So princes lose their renown if not —” (Pericles, Prince of Tyre)

definitions.text: “As jewels lose their glory if neglected So princes lose their renown if not —” (Pericles, Prince of Tyre)

blocks.clueFragment: “As jewels lose their glory if neglected So princes lose their renown if not —”
blocks.note: the quotation with one word removed
the source: Pericles, Act 2 scene 2, Simonides' court

explanation.walkthrough: The couplet rhymes the missing word with 'neglected', and the sense calls for its opposite: honoured.
explanation.definitionFit: Princes keep their reputation only when held in esteem, the opposite of jewels left uncared for.
